findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a proving step to the plan that demonstrates the failure-mode AC: e.g., temporarily decorate one test with `@pytest.mark.integration`, run the new collection-guard test, confirm it fails RED (collected count < 9), then remove the decorator — and include this as an explicit verification step or a paired AC.
evidence: The plan describes the test mechanism in prose ('Collecting by running the real selection — rather than grepping for marker text — is what makes it catch a marker added anywhere') but provides no step to empirically confirm the failure mode fires.
No AC or Testing section step says: add a marker, run the test, observe RED, remove the marker.
Taxonomy item 4 (fixture invalidity) applies: no described step exercises the claim that the test correctly detects the regression it is designed to catch.
findings.finding: The AC 'That test FAILS if a marker excluding either file from the default selection is added' has no corresponding proving step or command in the plan. An executor could implement a test that always returns 9 (e.g., hardcoded assertion, file-existence check, or a collection call without the `-m` filter) and every green AC would still pass. Without a described step that temporarily adds a marker, runs the new test, and confirms it goes RED, the failure-mode guarantee is unverified.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria — 'That test FAILS if a marker excluding either file from the default selection is added.'
scenarios: An agent writes `assert len(collected) == 9` where `collected` is built from a glob of the two files (always 9), not from a real pytest collection run — all green ACs pass but the guard is hollow.
An agent omits the `-m` flag in the subprocess call — the count is still 9 today, so green, but the test won't catch a future marker addition.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the Acceptance Criteria (or Testing section) a verification step such as: 'During implementation, confirm the guard is live by adding `@pytest.mark.integration` to one test in `test_core_optionality.py`, running `python -m pytest tests/unit/test_ci_workflow_parity.py -k test_optionality_files_collected_by_default_suite` and observing a RED failure, then reverting the marker.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Clarify and document whether the collection-count assertion should be `== 9` (exact, requiring update on additions) or `>= 9` (floor, catching only deletions/marking), and add an inline comment explaining the chosen policy so future contributors know how to maintain it.
evidence: Plan AC: 'asserts 9 items are collected'
Plan Testing section: 'asserts 9 items are collected'
ABSENCE: no guidance on whether equality or a floor check is intended, nor any note that the count must be bumped when tests are added
findings.finding: The hardcoded count `9` in the collection guard is a threshold expected to evolve as new optionality tests are added, but the plan does not specify whether the assertion should be `== 9` (strict) or `>= 9` (floor), nor does it document that the count must be manually updated when new tests are added to those files.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria: 'A checked-in test asserts … collect 9 items under `-m "not integration and not external"`'
scenarios: A contributor adds a 10th valid optionality test to `test_core_optionality.py`; the guard breaks with a confusing failure (`expected 9, got 10`), forcing them to hunt down the magic number.

findings.suggested_fix: Use `assert collected >= 9, f'Expected at least 9 optionality tests in default suite, got {collected}'` and add a comment: `# Floor: bump this when new tests are intentionally added to these files.` This catches the guard-deletion scenario while not breaking on legitimate additions.

findings.finding: The new collection-guard test in tests/unit/ will invoke pytest as a subprocess, but the plan does not state the @pytest.mark.allow_network precondition that the existing analogous test (test_external_isolation.py:51) requires for the same reason: 'subprocess pytest may touch local sockets'. The conftest.py _network_guard autouse fixture will intercept socket connections in tests/unit/ for any test lacking that marker, potentially causing the new test to fail in CI despite correct collection logic.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Clarify that the collection guard covers only pytest-marker exclusions, not CI YAML `paths:` filters; if the `paths:` threat vector is material, add a separate assertion (e.g. in `test_ci_workflow_parity.py`) that `_build-and-test.yml` does not carry a `paths:` key that would exclude optionality-test-only changes.
evidence: Plan (Testing): 'Collecting by running the real selection...is what makes it catch a marker added anywhere: file-level pytestmark, a decorator, or a conftest-applied mark.'
Plan (Context): 'A future contributor who adds @pytest.mark.integration, moves the files, or adds a paths: filter deletes the optionality guard with a fully GREEN build.'
A pytest --collect-only run is entirely unaware of _build-and-test.yml's trigger configuration; a paths: filter in that file is invisible to the proposed guard.
ABSENCE: no complementary check on the CI YAML paths: key is specified anywhere in the plan.
findings.finding: The plan claims the collection guard catches a future 'paths:' filter added to CI YAML as a threat vector, but a pytest-based collection test cannot detect a GitHub Actions `paths:` filter — that filter is evaluated by the Actions runner when deciding whether to trigger a job, not by pytest's marker deselection logic. The guard as specified covers only pytest-marker-based exclusions.
findings.location: Testing section: 'a future contributor who adds @pytest.mark.integration, moves the files, or adds a paths: filter deletes the optionality guard'
scenarios: A contributor adds `paths: ['src/**']` to the matrix job in _build-and-test.yml, making it skip on pure-test changes. The collection guard still passes (9 items collected). The optionality guard is silently absent from certain runs.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Change the AC (and implementation) from an exact `== 9` assertion to a lower-bound `>= 9` (or enumerate the specific test node-ids), so the guard remains durable when new tests are added to either file without creating false failures.
evidence: AC line: 'asserts 9 items are collected' — strict equality.
test_optional.py currently has 7 tests; test_core_optionality.py has 2. Any new test added to either file makes the guard fail spuriously.

The guard's actual purpose is 'all existing tests are still collected under default selection', not 'exactly 9 tests exist' — a >= 9 lower bound or a 'all previously-known items still present' check would be durable.
findings.finding: The AC hard-codes exactly 9 collected items (`asserts 9 items are collected`), but both target files can legitimately grow — a new helper test added to either file would break the guard with a false failure. The plan offers no guidance on how to handle future additions, which risks eroding trust in the guard (developers bump the number without scrutiny) or blocking valid contributions.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria: 'A checked-in test asserts tests/unit/test_core_optionality.py and tests/unit/test_optional.py collect 9 items under -m "not integration and not external".'
scenarios: A contributor adds a new test to test_optional.py (valid, unrelated to optionality markers). The collection guard fires with 'expected 9, got 10', breaking their otherwise-clean PR.
findings.suggested_fix: Assert `collected >= 9` (or check that all 9 known node-ids appear in the collected set) rather than `collected == 9`, and note in a comment that the bound should be updated when tests are intentionally removed.
